canonicalExplanation.summary: Array methods let you describe **what** you want instead of managing loop counters. `filter` keeps items that pass a test; `map` transforms every item into a new one; `reduce` combines all items into one value; `find` returns the first match; `some`/`every` answer yes/no questions. Each returns a **new** value — so use `forEach` (or a loop) for side effects, and don't call `map` when you ignore its result.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A course page must show the titles of published lessons in upper case. The loop version needs an empty array, an `if`, and a `push`. The pipeline version reads like the requirement. filter retains matching values, and map transforms each retained value in a separate step. In this lesson you'll construct and explain a transformation pipeline and compare it with an explicit loop.

```predict
{"question": "`[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(n => n % 2 === 0).map(n => n * 10)` returns…", "options": ["[10, 20, 30, 40]", "[20, 40]"], "answer": 1, "why": "filter keeps 2 and 4; map turns them into 20 and 40."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Control flow and functions** module, **Data-structure choice**, **Arrays and indexed data**, and **Function declarations, expressions and arrows**.

sections.heading: The model: one job per step
sections.body:
```js
const lessons = [
  { title: "Arrays", published: true, minutes: 12 },
  { title: "Maps", published: false, minutes: 9 },
  { title: "Loops", published: true, minutes: 15 },
];

const titles = lessons
  .filter((l) => l.published)            // keep: Arrays, Loops
  .map((l) => l.title.toUpperCase());    // ["ARRAYS", "LOOPS"]

const totalMinutes = lessons.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l.minutes, 0);  // 36
const firstDraft = lessons.find((l) => !l.published);                 // Maps
const anyLong = lessons.some((l) => l.minutes > 14);                  // true
```

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `filter`. | new array of items that pass. |
| `map`. | new array, same length, transformed. |
| `reduce`. | one combined value (give an initial value!). |
| `find`. | first match or undefined. |
| `some` / `every`. | true/false. |
| `forEach`. | undefined — for side effects only. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why pass `0` as reduce's second argument?", "answer": "It's the starting total. Without it, reduce uses the first item (an object here) as the start — and throws on an empty array."}
```

sections.heading: Pipeline or loop?

includes: Build pipelines with filter, map, reduce, find, some and every.
Compare a pipeline with an explicit loop and avoid map for side effects.

outcomes: Construct and explain a transformation pipeline and compare it with an explicit loop.

examples.title: Filter, then map
examples.situation: filter retains matching values and map transforms each retained value in a separate step.
walkthrough: **filter retains matching values:** `lessons.filter(l => l.published)` keeps Arrays and Loops.
**map transforms each retained value:** `.map(l => l.title.toUpperCase())` produces ["ARRAYS", "LOOPS"].
**Compare the loop:** `const out = []; for (const l of lessons) { if (l.published) out.push(l.title.toUpperCase()); }` will give the same result with more bookkeeping.
examples.result: The pipeline returns ["ARRAYS", "LOOPS"] and reads like the requirement: published lessons, titles in capitals.

examples.title: The reduce without a start
examples.situation: `const total = carts.reduce((sum, c) => sum + c.price);` crashes when carts is empty and gives "[object Object]20"-style nonsense otherwise.
walkthrough: Without an initial value, the first item (an object) becomes sum.
An empty array has no first item, so reduce throws TypeError.
examples.result: Totals are correct numbers, and an empty cart totals 0.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: map should be used for side effects when its returned array is ignored.
misconceptions.correction: map exists to build a new array from transformed values. When you only need side effects, use forEach or a for...of loop; ignoring map's result wastes work and misleads readers.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the "Pipeline or loop?" predict, what does the ignored map produce?

analogy.example: A pipeline is like a **factory line**: the first station removes faulty parts (filter), the next paints every remaining part (map), and the last packs them into one box (reduce). Each station has one clear job.
usefulFor: reading the line as a sentence
limitations: Factory lines run in parallel; array methods run step by step.
forEach is like a station that inspects parts but produces nothing.

steps.explanation: The pipeline starts from all three lessons.
filter retains matching values — the published lessons.
map transforms each retained value in a separate step.

remediation.explanation: Say the requirement aloud: "keep X, change each to Y, combine into Z". Map each phrase to filter, map, reduce. If you need side effects or an early break, use a loop.

recap.summary: To construct and explain a transformation pipeline, chain filter (keep), map (transform), reduce (combine, with an initial value), find, some and every — each returning a new value — and use forEach or a loop for side effects. Compare with an explicit loop and pick what reads more clearly.
retrievalPrompts: Why give reduce an initial value?
When should you not use map?
